criterion_notes.c1: Examines household and community piped drinking-water supply (and municipal sewerage/drainage interface) across four independent community water systems (SIAs) and the municipal utility (SAPAHUA) in Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca, Mexico.
criterion_notes.c2: Satisfies Criterion 2 under BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, it analyzes local water governance institutions (SIAs), the municipal operating agency (SAPAHUA), and non-recognition under the National Waters Law (LAN). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it examines concrete rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access: (1) utility ownership and regulatory structure (autonomous community-owned SIAs with Conagua concessions and written/customary operational rules vs. municipal utility control/takeover), (2) tariff, metering, and cost-recovery rules (flat monthly fees vs. metered consumption with tiered charges, extraordinary assembly levies, and valve-based rationing), (3) disconnection/enforcement constraints (non-paying users invoking the constitutional human right to water, preventing SIAs from cutting off service), and (4) agrarian/clandestine land-tenure and administrative-jurisdiction boundaries restricting SIA network extension to peripheral settlers.
criterion_notes.c3: Qualitative comparative case study of four independent water systems (two urban colonies and two rural municipal agencies) based on 20 in-depth key-informant interviews with current and former local water authorities, community actors, and municipal/SAPAHUA officials, triangulated with census (INEGI) and municipal utility (SAPAHUA) records. Per protocol safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are included for mechanism synthesis regardless of lacking quantitative effect sizes.
criterion_notes.c4: Reports concrete access and service outcomes at both locality and household-connection levels, including piped water and drainage connection counts, municipal-wide coverage shares (88 localities/70% served by SAPAHUA, 38 localities/23% by SIAs, 27 localities without continuous supply), intermittent supply schedules (days and hours per week), monthly household tariffs and fee-collection vs. electricity cost balances, unserved peripheral growth areas, and perceived/reported declines in water quantity and quality where SIAs ceded control to the municipal utility.
criterion_notes.c5: Population/unit of analysis (four SIA systems/localities serving 1,200 to 5,200 residents each within Huajuapan de León's 153 localities, informed by 20 key-informant interviews and locality connection records), exposure (independent user-owned utility governance, internal tariff/metering/rationing rules, non-disconnection under human-right-to-water claims, and jurisdictional/tenure boundaries vs. municipal utility), outcome (piped water coverage, supply continuity/hours, affordability/cost recovery, and quality/quantity retention), and study design (qualitative multiple-case study) are all clearly identifiable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is in Spanish with an English title and abstract. Per Criterion 10, Spanish-to-English translation from the complete, machine-readable 53-page PDF is directly feasible and the study provides important empirical socio-legal evidence on community vs. municipal utility ownership, tariff/disconnection rules, and peri-urban tenure/jurisdictional boundaries; translation method and translator should be logged in extraction_note during data extraction.

evidence_quotes.quote: Using a qualitative methodology, four cases were studied with a total of twenty in-depth interviews with representatives of citizen committees and municipal authorities in charge of water management.

De acuerdo con la investigación de campo y datos del Sistema Administrador de Agua Potable y Alcantarillado de la Ciudad de Huajuapan de León (SAPAHUA, 2018), el gobierno municipal abastece a 88 localidades y los SIAs a 38, por lo que existen 27 localidades sin suministro continuo de agua.

En entrevistas con exintegrantes de los comités de agua de San Mateo y San Diego se evidenció que esta situación ya sucedió en sus localidades, donde entregaron el control de su SIA al gobierno municipal, y la cantidad y calidad del agua que reciben ahora es inferior a lo que les abastecía su propio sistema.

raw_response.exposure: Independent community-owned water system (SIA) governance and regulatory structure (vs. municipal operating utility SAPAHUA and non-recognition under the National Waters Law), including internal tariff/metering rules, valve rationing rules, non-disconnection constraints under human-right-to-water claims, and communal vs. clandestine private land-tenure/jurisdictional boundaries.
raw_response.outcome: Household piped-water connection coverage and municipal locality coverage shares, service continuity (days and hours of supply per week), monthly tariffs and cost-recovery balances, peripheral unserved demand, and water quantity/quality retention vs. post-municipalization deterioration.
raw_response.population_and_sample: Four independent water systems (SIAs) in Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca, Mexico—two urban localities (Fraccionamiento Jardines del Sur, pop. 1,200; Colonia del Maestro, pop. 5,200) and two rural municipal agencies (Santa María Xochixtlapilco, pop. 4,100; Santa Teresa, pop. 4,000)—within a municipality of 153 localities (77,547 inhabitants), studied via 20 in-depth interviews (16 local SIA informants and 4 municipal/SAPAHUA officials) plus census and utility records.
raw_response.rationale: This empirical qualitative comparative case study examines household and community drinking-water service access across four user-governed independent water systems (SIAs) and the municipal water utility (SAPAHUA) in Huajuapan de León, Oaxaca, Mexico. It satisfies Criterion 2 under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope by investigating utility ownership/regulatory structure (autonomous community utilities lacking statutory recognition under the National Waters Law vs. municipal utility takeover), tariff and metering rules, human-right-to-water constraints preventing disconnection for non-payment, and agrarian/clandestine tenure and jurisdictional boundaries affecting peripheral connections. It provides primary qualitative interview evidence triangulated with administrative/census coverage, continuity, and tariff outcomes, and its Spanish full text is readily translatable per Criterion 10.
raw_response.study_design: Qualitative comparative case study (4 cases; 20 in-depth key-informant interviews triangulated with census and municipal utility data)
